title: How I Find Problems to Solve as a Staff Engineer
excerpt: How listening broadly turns everyday problems into useful project ideas.
content_html:
Note: this post was revised after publishing for increased clarity, based on reader feedback.

“How do you find problems worth working on?” a senior engineer I mentor asked me recently. He’s trying to make the jump to staff engineer and realized that the role isn’t just about doing the work he’s assigned. He also needs to get involved in figuring out what his team and org should be building.

Someone else had suggested blocking out time in his calendar to think about the bigger picture. He’d tried that, but hadn’t found it productive, so he asked if I had any alternatives.

I told him I rarely find good problems by staring at a blank page and trying to “think strategically.” Instead, I act like a sponge. I listen to the stream of day-to-day noise, absorb the problems people are having and let them sit in the back of my mind. Over time, some fade away while connections begin to appear between others that initially seemed unrelated. Eventually, I start to see what’s really slowing people down and what my team or I can do about it.

I’ve worked with many engineers who’ve never really tried this. They wait for managers or leads to identify opportunities, then demonstrate their value by solving the hardest assigned problems. That can absolutely lead to promotion. But the projects that have made the biggest impression in my career were the ones where I found and solved an important problem my leaders did not yet realize existed.

One caveat: my experience comes mainly from working on infrastructure and developer tools at large companies, on teams where engineers have a lot of bottom-up autonomy to influence their roadmaps. In a more top-down environment, there may simply be less room to work this way.

Absorb problems, not requests

People love talking about the problems they are facing: in meetings, chat threads, presentations and email. They explain why their work is hard, complain about what slows them down and describe what they wish they could do.

When something overlaps with my area, I start pulling on the thread. I might ask, “If X existed, would it solve your problem?” or point them at an existing feature in a product I own and ask how much of their use case it covers.

Users often ask for a particular solution instead of explaining their root issue. Rather than taking the request at face value, I keep digging until I understand what they are trying to accomplish and why existing products do not work for them.

As a natural introvert, this sort of ambient listening works particularly well for me. I don’t need to fill my calendar with speculative meetings just to find ideas; there is already an enormous amount of useful information flowing around me during a normal week.

When a problem seems worth exploring, though, I become more active; I need to see how it affects the team’s day-to-day work. I’ll sit with them as they walk me through their workflows and the bugs they’re investigating. When I can, I’ll try working through some of those bugs myself. Seeing the problem firsthand makes it easier to separate what the team actually needs from the solution they asked for.

I also seek out people who see more of the organization than I do: those who own critical systems, work across several teams or have particularly deep insight into the work downstream of my team. I’ll arrange a 1:1 or coffee chat and ask about interesting problems they’ve come across. They may have already seen the same issue in several places and started connecting the dots, giving me a head start on patterns I might otherwise have taken much longer to notice.

Let problems accumulate

Several times, I’ve been burned by moving too fast. I became excited by a request from a vocal team, built the feature and watched them barely use it. Their priorities had changed, or the request had come from a one-off investigation that no longer mattered. How eager a team was in that moment wasn’t the same as how important the feature was relative to everything else my product needed to support. By hyperfocusing on their request, I lost sight of the bigger picture.

That taught me to let potential problems pile up. Listening the way I do leaves me with far more of them than I could possibly solve, and not all deserve action. Most don’t need to turn into projects the first time I hear about them; waiting can be a superpower.

Waiting means the same problem might pop up independently in different teams, making it a higher priority to solve. Or problems that look different on the surface might turn out to have the same shape, so I can address several use cases in one shot. Or, as I’ve learned painfully, the requesting team didn’t even care that much in the first place.

Instead, I make a mental note and revisit the problem if it comes up again. Other engineers I know write this sort of thing down more systematically. The mechanism is a personal choice: everyone has to figure out what works for them. What matters is keeping unresolved problems around long enough for more evidence to accumulate.

Find the common shape

Waiting helps me collect evidence, but that alone doesn’t tell me what to build. I still need to work out whether the problems I’ve retained are genuinely related and what, if anything, could address them together.

Perfetto, the performance debugging tool I work on, is a good example. It displays recordings of system activity on a timeline made up of rows called “tracks.” Over a couple of years, teams kept asking for small, specific additions to the UI. One wanted a command to keep their preferred tracks pinned to the top of the screen; the next team wanted the same, but for a completely different set of tracks. Others wanted Perfetto to open already zoomed in on a particular part of a recording, or to show a custom aggregation tuned to what they cared about. A few had stopped waiting for us and built elaborate workarounds with bookmarklets.1

By the time enough of these had piled up, my head was the usual tangle: the requests themselves, the constraints on each and a handful of half-formed solutions. I’ve learned not to force a solution by just sitting at a desk and thinking. Instead, my best untangling happens on long, aimless walks around London, where connections come more easily when I’m not trying to force them.

What I eventually realized was that none of these teams really wanted the specific feature they’d asked for. Each wanted to personalize Perfetto for their own workflow without imposing their choices on everyone else. The underlying need wasn’t any one feature but rather the ability to extend the UI. When a connection like that finally clicks, it’s one of the best feelings in the job: several awkward requests collapse into a single idea, and possibilities open up that none of them hinted at on their own.

That feeling, though, is exactly when I have to be careful, because a common shape is only a hypothesis and elegance is not evidence. When it happened with extending the UI it turned out to be real, but I’ve been fooled before.

In another recent case I was convinced that building a transparent caching system for querying Perfetto traces would solve issues with sharing large traces and repeated queries. It was only as I wrote the RFC and built a prototype that I realized the elegance was a lie: the two problems wanted genuinely different solutions. I reluctantly split the design in two, both halves of which have since shipped.2

Pressure-test before building

You’d think this would be the moment I start building, but it usually isn’t. How far I go depends on how sure I am that the idea works and that people actually want it.

If something is useful and low-risk enough, I act straight away: I send the change and let my manager know. When I’m unsure whether an idea will work or how much effort it will take, I build a throwaway prototype instead; it exposes the failure points and gives me something concrete for others to react to. And when an idea is big but I’m convinced by it, I commit to the full effort: weeks or months of work and the hard yards of building support across other engineers and teams.

Through all of it, I’m not only trying to convince other people; I’m also trying to convince myself. Sometimes the honest answer is to stop: if people don’t see the value I do, or we hit a major technical wall, I’d rather drop the idea now than build something no one uses or that becomes a maintenance nightmare. And sometimes it holds up but the timing is wrong, so I park it, ready to spring into action the day it becomes an org priority.

When an idea does hold up, I don’t necessarily need to be the person who builds it. I might implement it, someone else on my team might, or it might change what the org focuses on. Finding and shaping the right problem can have an impact even when I don’t own the implementation.

The Perfetto extensions idea was worth that full effort. We were already building plugins to modularize the UI, but they weren’t enough: teams had to open source all their plugin code, which wasn’t an option for many internal use cases. So before building anything new, I took the problem and my proposal to my manager, teammates and the client teams. I ended up writing two RFCs, having several 1:1s and giving a couple of talks, refining it as the feedback came in.

In the end, I designed and implemented macros as “lightweight extensions”: a way to automate actions in the UI without writing a plugin. Extension servers took the idea further by letting teams share their macros.

Instead of implementing every requested feature ourselves, we gave teams ways to adapt Perfetto to their own needs. Dozens of teams inside Google now use macros and extension servers, and several other companies use extension servers internally too.

Solving useful problems helps me find the next one

The more often I go through this process, the easier it becomes. When I show genuine interest in someone’s problem, ask useful questions or help solve it, they remember. They start coming to me earlier and bring me into conversations with other people facing related issues.

That gives me a wider view of what is happening across the organization, making it easier to spot patterns and build things people actually need. Solving one of those problems brings me into more conversations, and the loop continues.

Those successes build the kind of trust that comes from long-term stewardship. Early on, I had to turn many of these ideas into something real myself to prove that my judgment was sound. Over time, my manager and org gave more weight to my assessment of what mattered. That allowed me to influence the roadmap without needing to own every project.

This differs from the idea that becoming a staff engineer means replacing technical work with meetings and coordination. For me, conversations are inputs into what I build, not the end result.

Conclusion

That is what I wanted my mentee to understand: finding problems worth solving isn’t separate from the rest of the job. It comes from staying engaged with people’s work long enough to see what no single request can show you.

sentences.en: I also seek out people who see more of the organization than I do: those who own critical systems, work across several teams or have particularly deep insight into the work downstream of my team.
sentences.zh: 我还寻找比我更了解组织的人：那些拥有关键系统、跨多个团队工作或对我团队下游工作有特别深入了解的人。

sentences.en: I’ll arrange a 1:1 or coffee chat and ask about interesting problems they’ve come across.
sentences.zh: 我会安排一对一或咖啡聊天，询问他们遇到的有趣问题。

sentences.en: They may have already seen the same issue in several places and started connecting the dots, giving me a head start on patterns I might otherwise have taken much longer to notice.
sentences.zh: 他们可能已经在多个地方看到了同样的问题，并开始将这些点联系起来，让我在模式上领先一步，否则我可能需要更长时间才能注意到。

blocks.html_en: Let problems accumulate

sentences.en: Let problems accumulate
sentences.zh: 让问题不断积累

blocks.html_en: Several times, I’ve been burned by moving too fast. I became excited by a request from a vocal team, built the feature and watched them barely use it. Their priorities had changed, or the request had come from a one-off investigation that no longer mattered. How eager a team was in that moment wasn’t the same as how important the feature was relative to everything else my product needed to support. By hyperfocusing on their request, I lost sight of the bigger picture.

sentences.en: Several times, I’ve been burned by moving too fast.
sentences.zh: 有好几次，我因动作太快而被烫伤。

sentences.en: I became excited by a request from a vocal team, built the feature and watched them barely use it.
sentences.zh: 我对一个声音团队的请求感到兴奋，构建了这个功能，然后看着他们几乎不使用它。

sentences.en: Their priorities had changed, or the request had come from a one-off investigation that no longer mattered.
sentences.zh: 他们的优先事项发生了变化，或者请求来自不再重要的一次性调查。

sentences.en: How eager a team was in that moment wasn’t the same as how important the feature was relative to everything else my product needed to support.
sentences.zh: 团队在那一刻的渴望程度并不等同于该功能相对于我的产品需要支持的其他所有内容的重要性。

sentences.en: By hyperfocusing on their request, I lost sight of the bigger picture.
sentences.zh: 由于过度关注他们的要求，我忽视了更大的前景。

blocks.html_en: That taught me to let potential problems pile up. Listening the way I do leaves me with far more of them than I could possibly solve, and not all deserve action. Most don’t need to turn into projects the first time I hear about them; waiting can be a superpower.

sentences.en: That taught me to let potential problems pile up.
sentences.zh: 这教会了我要让潜在的问题堆积起来。

sentences.en: Listening the way I do leaves me with far more of them than I could possibly solve, and not all deserve action.
sentences.zh: 按照我的方式倾听，我遇到的问题远远超出了我所能解决的范围，而且并非所有问题都值得采取行动。

sentences.en: Most don’t need to turn into projects the first time I hear about them; waiting can be a superpower.
sentences.zh: 大多数人不需要在我第一次听说它们时就将其转变为项目；等待可以是一种超能力。

blocks.html_en: Waiting means the same problem might pop up independently in different teams, making it a higher priority to solve. Or problems that look different on the surface might turn out to have the same shape, so I can address several use cases in one shot. Or, as I’ve learned painfully, the requesting team didn’t even care that much in the first place.

sentences.en: Waiting means the same problem might pop up independently in different teams, making it a higher priority to solve.
sentences.zh: 等待意味着相同的问题可能会在不同的团队中独立出现，从而使其成为更优先解决的问题。

sentences.en: Or problems that look different on the surface might turn out to have the same shape, so I can address several use cases in one shot.
sentences.zh: 或者表面上看起来不同的问题可能最终具有相同的形状，因此我可以一次性解决多个用例。

sentences.en: Or, as I’ve learned painfully, the requesting team didn’t even care that much in the first place.
sentences.zh: 或者，正如我痛苦地了解到的那样，提出请求的团队一开始根本就没有那么在意。

blocks.html_en: Instead, I make a mental note and revisit the problem if it comes up again. Other engineers I know write this sort of thing down more systematically. The mechanism is a personal choice: everyone has to figure out what works for them. What matters is keeping unresolved problems around long enough for more evidence to accumulate.

sentences.en: Instead, I make a mental note and revisit the problem if it comes up again.
sentences.zh: 相反，我会在心里记下并在问题再次出现时重新审视该问题。

sentences.en: Other engineers I know write this sort of thing down more systematically.
sentences.zh: 我认识的其他工程师更系统地记录了这类事情。

sentences.en: The mechanism is a personal choice: everyone has to figure out what works for them.
sentences.zh: 该机制是个人选择：每个人都必须找出适合自己的机制。

sentences.en: What matters is keeping unresolved problems around long enough for more evidence to accumulate.
sentences.zh: 重要的是让未解决的问题保持足够长的时间，以便积累更多证据。

blocks.html_en: Find the common shape

sentences.en: Find the common shape
sentences.zh: 找出共同的形状

blocks.html_en: Waiting helps me collect evidence, but that alone doesn’t tell me what to build. I still need to work out whether the problems I’ve retained are genuinely related and what, if anything, could address them together.

sentences.en: Waiting helps me collect evidence, but that alone doesn’t tell me what to build.
sentences.zh: 等待可以帮助我收集证据，但仅凭这一点并不能告诉我要构建什么。

sentences.en: I still need to work out whether the problems I’ve retained are genuinely related and what, if anything, could address them together.
sentences.zh: 我仍然需要弄清楚我保留的问题是否真正相关，如果有的话，可以一起解决它们。

blocks.html_en: Perfetto, the performance debugging tool I work on, is a good example. It displays recordings of system activity on a timeline made up of rows called “tracks.” Over a couple of years, teams kept asking for small, specific additions to the UI. One wanted a command to keep their preferred tracks pinned to the top of the screen; the next team wanted the same, but for a completely different set of tracks. Others wanted Perfetto to open already zoomed in on a particular part of a recording, or to show a custom aggregation tuned to what they cared about. A few had stopped waiting for us and built elaborate workarounds with bookmarklets.1

sentences.en: Perfetto, the performance debugging tool I work on, is a good example.
sentences.zh: 我使用的性能调试工具 Perfetto 就是一个很好的例子。

sentences.en: It displays recordings of system activity on a timeline made up of rows called “tracks.”
sentences.zh: 它在由称为“轨道”的行组成的时间线上显示系统活动的记录。

sentences.en: Over a couple of years, teams kept asking for small, specific additions to the UI.
sentences.zh: 几年来，团队不断要求对 UI 进行小的、具体的添加。

sentences.en: One wanted a command to keep their preferred tracks pinned to the top of the screen; the next team wanted the same, but for a completely different set of tracks.
sentences.zh: 人们想要一个命令来将他们喜欢的曲目固定在屏幕顶部；下一个团队想要同样的东西，但要制作一组完全不同的曲目。

sentences.en: Others wanted Perfetto to open already zoomed in on a particular part of a recording, or to show a custom aggregation tuned to what they cared about.
sentences.zh: 其他人希望 Perfetto 打开已经放大的录音的特定部分，或者显示根据他们关心的内容调整的自定义聚合。

sentences.en: A few had stopped waiting for us and built elaborate workarounds with bookmarklets.1
sentences.zh: 一些人已经停止等待我们，并使用书签构建了精心设计的解决方法。1

blocks.html_en: By the time enough of these had piled up, my head was the usual tangle: the requests themselves, the constraints on each and a handful of half-formed solutions. I’ve learned not to force a solution by just sitting at a desk and thinking. Instead, my best untangling happens on long, aimless walks around London, where connections come more easily when I’m not trying to force them.

sentences.en: By the time enough of these had piled up, my head was the usual tangle: the requests themselves, the constraints on each and a handful of half-formed solutions.
sentences.zh: 当这些都堆积起来时，我的头脑又像往常一样混乱：请求本身、每个请求的限制以及一些半成形的解决方案。

sentences.en: I’ve learned not to force a solution by just sitting at a desk and thinking.
sentences.zh: 我学会了不要仅仅坐在办公桌前思考来强迫解决方案。

sentences.en: Instead, my best untangling happens on long, aimless walks around London, where connections come more easily when I’m not trying to force them.
sentences.zh: 相反，我最好的解开纠结的方式是在伦敦漫无目的地散步，当我不试图强迫他们时，联系会更容易。

blocks.html_en: What I eventually realized was that none of these teams really wanted the specific feature they’d asked for. Each wanted to personalize Perfetto for their own workflow without imposing their choices on everyone else. The underlying need wasn’t any one feature but rather the ability to extend the UI. When a connection like that finally clicks, it’s one of the best feelings in the job: several awkward requests collapse into a single idea, and possibilities open up that none of them hinted at on their own.

sentences.en: What I eventually realized was that none of these teams really wanted the specific feature they’d asked for.
sentences.zh: 我最终意识到，这些团队中没有一个真正想要他们所要求的特定功能。

sentences.en: Each wanted to personalize Perfetto for their own workflow without imposing their choices on everyone else.
sentences.zh: 每个人都希望针对自己的工作流程个性化 Perfetto，而不是将自己的选择强加给其他人。

sentences.en: The underlying need wasn’t any one feature but rather the ability to extend the UI.
sentences.zh: 根本需求不是任何一项功能，而是扩展 UI 的能力。

sentences.en: When a connection like that finally clicks, it’s one of the best feelings in the job: several awkward requests collapse into a single idea, and possibilities open up that none of them hinted at on their own.
sentences.zh: 当这样的联系最终产生时，这是工作中最好的感觉之一：几个尴尬的请求崩溃成一个想法，并且出现了他们自己都没有暗示过的可能性。

blocks.html_en: That feeling, though, is exactly when I have to be careful, because a common shape is only a hypothesis and elegance is not evidence. When it happened with extending the UI it turned out to be real, but I’ve been fooled before.

sentences.en: That feeling, though, is exactly when I have to be careful, because a common shape is only a hypothesis and elegance is not evidence.
sentences.zh: 然而，这种感觉正是我必须小心的时候，因为常见的形状只是一个假设，优雅并不是证据。

sentences.en: When it happened with extending the UI it turned out to be real, but I’ve been fooled before.
sentences.zh: 当扩展 UI 时，它被证明是真实的，但我以前被愚弄过。

blocks.html_en: In another recent case I was convinced that building a transparent caching system for querying Perfetto traces would solve issues with sharing large traces and repeated queries. It was only as I wrote the RFC and built a prototype that I realized the elegance was a lie: the two problems wanted genuinely different solutions. I reluctantly split the design in two, both halves of which have since shipped.2

sentences.en: In another recent case I was convinced that building a transparent caching system for querying Perfetto traces would solve issues with sharing large traces and repeated queries.
sentences.zh: 在最近的另一个案例中，我确信构建一个用于查询 Perfetto 跟踪的透明缓存系统将解决共享大型跟踪和重复查询的问题。

sentences.en: It was only as I wrote the RFC and built a prototype that I realized the elegance was a lie: the two problems wanted genuinely different solutions.
sentences.zh: 直到我编写 RFC 并构建原型时，我才意识到这种优雅是一个谎言：这两个问题需要真正不同的解决方案。

sentences.en: I reluctantly split the design in two, both halves of which have since shipped.2
sentences.zh: 我不情愿地将设计分成两部分，两半都已发货。2

blocks.html_en: Pressure-test before building

sentences.en: Pressure-test before building
sentences.zh: 施工前进行压力测试

blocks.html_en: You’d think this would be the moment I start building, but it usually isn’t. How far I go depends on how sure I am that the idea works and that people actually want it.

sentences.en: You’d think this would be the moment I start building, but it usually isn’t.
sentences.zh: 你可能认为这就是我开始构建的时刻，但通常不是。

sentences.en: How far I go depends on how sure I am that the idea works and that people actually want it.
sentences.zh: 我能走多远取决于我对这个想法是否有效以及人们是否真正想要它的确信程度。

blocks.html_en: If something is useful and low-risk enough, I act straight away: I send the change and let my manager know. When I’m unsure whether an idea will work or how much effort it will take, I build a throwaway prototype instead; it exposes the failure points and gives me something concrete for others to react to. And when an idea is big but I’m convinced by it, I commit to the full effort: weeks or months of work and the hard yards of building support across other engineers and teams.

sentences.en: If something is useful and low-risk enough, I act straight away: I send the change and let my manager know.
sentences.zh: 如果某件事有用且风险足够低，我会立即采取行动：发送更改并让我的经理知道。

sentences.en: When I’m unsure whether an idea will work or how much effort it will take, I build a throwaway prototype instead; it exposes the failure points and gives me something concrete for others to react to.
sentences.zh: 当我不确定一个想法是否可行或需要付出多少努力时，我会构建一个一次性原型；它暴露了失败点，并为我提供了一些具体的内容供其他人做出反应。

sentences.en: And when an idea is big but I’m convinced by it, I commit to the full effort: weeks or months of work and the hard yards of building support across other engineers and teams.
sentences.zh: 当一个想法很大但我被它说服时，我会全力以赴：数周或数月的工作以及在其他工程师和团队之间建立支持的艰苦努力。

blocks.html_en: Through all of it, I’m not only trying to convince other people; I’m also trying to convince myself. Sometimes the honest answer is to stop: if people don’t see the value I do, or we hit a major technical wall, I’d rather drop the idea now than build something no one uses or that becomes a maintenance nightmare. And sometimes it holds up but the timing is wrong, so I park it, ready to spring into action the day it becomes an org priority.

sentences.en: Through all of it, I’m not only trying to convince other people; I’m also trying to convince myself.
sentences.zh: 通过这一切，我不仅试图说服其他人，而且还试图说服其他人。我也在努力说服自己。

sentences.en: Sometimes the honest answer is to stop: if people don’t see the value I do, or we hit a major technical wall, I’d rather drop the idea now than build something no one uses or that becomes a maintenance nightmare.
sentences.zh: 有时，诚实的答案是停止：如果人们看不到我所做的价值，或者我们遇到了主要的技术障碍，我宁愿现在放弃这个想法，也不愿构建一些没有人使用或成为维护噩梦的东西。

sentences.en: And sometimes it holds up but the timing is wrong, so I park it, ready to spring into action the day it becomes an org priority.
sentences.zh: 有时它会持续下去，但时机不对，所以我把它搁置起来，准备在它成为组织优先事项的那一天立即采取行动。

blocks.html_en: When an idea does hold up, I don’t necessarily need to be the person who builds it. I might implement it, someone else on my team might, or it might change what the org focuses on. Finding and shaping the right problem can have an impact even when I don’t own the implementation.

sentences.en: When an idea does hold up, I don’t necessarily need to be the person who builds it.
sentences.zh: 当一个想法确实成立时，我不一定是构建它的人。

sentences.en: I might implement it, someone else on my team might, or it might change what the org focuses on.
sentences.zh: 我可能会实施它，我团队中的其他人可能会实施它，或者它可能会改变组织的重点。

sentences.en: Finding and shaping the right problem can have an impact even when I don’t own the implementation.
sentences.zh: 即使我不负责实施，找到并塑造正确的问题也会产生影响。

blocks.html_en: The Perfetto extensions idea was worth that full effort. We were already building plugins to modularize the UI, but they weren’t enough: teams had to open source all their plugin code, which wasn’t an option for many internal use cases. So before building anything new, I took the problem and my proposal to my manager, teammates and the client teams. I ended up writing two RFCs, having several 1:1s and giving a couple of talks, refining it as the feedback came in.

sentences.en: The Perfetto extensions idea was worth that full effort.
sentences.zh: Perfetto 扩展的想法值得全力以赴。

sentences.en: We were already building plugins to modularize the UI, but they weren’t enough: teams had to open source all their plugin code, which wasn’t an option for many internal use cases.
sentences.zh: 我们已经在构建插件来模块化 UI，但它们还不够：团队必须开源所有插件代码，这对于许多内部用例来说不是一个选择。

sentences.en: So before building anything new, I took the problem and my proposal to my manager, teammates and the client teams.
sentences.zh: 因此，在构建任何新产品之前，我将问题和建议提交给我的经理、队友和客户团队。

sentences.en: I ended up writing two RFCs, having several 1:1s and giving a couple of talks, refining it as the feedback came in.
sentences.zh: 我最终写了两份 RFC，进行了几次一对一讨论并进行了几次演讲，并根据反馈进行了改进。

blocks.html_en: In the end, I designed and implemented macros as “lightweight extensions”: a way to automate actions in the UI without writing a plugin. Extension servers took the idea further by letting teams share their macros.

sentences.en: In the end, I designed and implemented macros as “lightweight extensions”: a way to automate actions in the UI without writing a plugin.
sentences.zh: 最后，我将宏设计并实现为“轻量级扩展”：一种无需编写插件即可在 UI 中自动执行操作的方法。

sentences.en: Extension servers took the idea further by letting teams share their macros.
sentences.zh: 扩展服务器通过让团队共享他们的宏来进一步发展这个想法。

blocks.html_en: Instead of implementing every requested feature ourselves, we gave teams ways to adapt Perfetto to their own needs. Dozens of teams inside Google now use macros and extension servers, and several other companies use extension servers internally too.

sentences.en: Instead of implementing every requested feature ourselves, we gave teams ways to adapt Perfetto to their own needs.
sentences.zh: 我们没有自己实现每个要求的功能，而是为团队提供了根据自己的需求调整 Perfetto 的方法。

sentences.en: Dozens of teams inside Google now use macros and extension servers, and several other companies use extension servers internally too.
sentences.zh: Google 内部的数十个团队现在使用宏和扩展服务器，其他几家公司也在内部使用扩展服务器。

blocks.html_en: Solving useful problems helps me find the next one

sentences.en: Solving useful problems helps me find the next one
sentences.zh: 解决有用的问题可以帮助我找到下一个问题

blocks.html_en: The more often I go through this process, the easier it becomes. When I show genuine interest in someone’s problem, ask useful questions or help solve it, they remember. They start coming to me earlier and bring me into conversations with other people facing related issues.

sentences.en: The more often I go through this process, the easier it becomes.
sentences.zh: 我越经常经历这个过程，它就会变得越容易。

sentences.en: When I show genuine interest in someone’s problem, ask useful questions or help solve it, they remember.
sentences.zh: 当我对某人的问题表现出真正的兴趣、提出有用的问题或帮助解决问题时，他们会记住。

sentences.en: They start coming to me earlier and bring me into conversations with other people facing related issues.
sentences.zh: 他们开始更早地来找我，让我与面临相关问题的其他人进行对话。

blocks.html_en: That gives me a wider view of what is happening across the organization, making it easier to spot patterns and build things people actually need. Solving one of those problems brings me into more conversations, and the loop continues.

sentences.en: That gives me a wider view of what is happening across the organization, making it easier to spot patterns and build things people actually need.
sentences.zh: 这让我能够更广泛地了解整个组织正在发生的事情，从而更容易发现模式并构建人们真正需要的东西。

sentences.en: Solving one of those problems brings me into more conversations, and the loop continues.
sentences.zh: 解决其中一个问题会让我进行更多对话，并且循环继续。

blocks.html_en: Those successes build the kind of trust that comes from long-term stewardship. Early on, I had to turn many of these ideas into something real myself to prove that my judgment was sound. Over time, my manager and org gave more weight to my assessment of what mattered. That allowed me to influence the roadmap without needing to own every project.

sentences.en: Those successes build the kind of trust that comes from long-term stewardship.
sentences.zh: 这些成功建立了来自长期管理的信任。

sentences.en: Early on, I had to turn many of these ideas into something real myself to prove that my judgment was sound.
sentences.zh: 早期，我必须亲自将其中许多想法变成现实，以证明我的判断是正确的。

sentences.en: Over time, my manager and org gave more weight to my assessment of what mattered.
sentences.zh: 随着时间的推移，我的经理和组织更加重视我对重要事项的评估。

sentences.en: That allowed me to influence the roadmap without needing to own every project.
sentences.zh: 这使我能够影响路线图，而无需拥有每个项目。

blocks.html_en: This differs from the idea that becoming a staff engineer means replacing technical work with meetings and coordination. For me, conversations are inputs into what I build, not the end result.

sentences.en: This differs from the idea that becoming a staff engineer means replacing technical work with meetings and coordination.
sentences.zh: 这与成为一名高级工程师意味着用会议和协调取代技术工作的想法不同。

sentences.en: For me, conversations are inputs into what I build, not the end result.
sentences.zh: 对我来说，对话是对我构建的内容的输入，而不是最终结果。

blocks.html_en: Conclusion

sentences.en: Conclusion
sentences.zh: 结论

blocks.html_en: That is what I wanted my mentee to understand: finding problems worth solving isn’t separate from the rest of the job. It comes from staying engaged with people’s work long enough to see what no single request can show you.

sentences.en: That is what I wanted my mentee to understand: finding problems worth solving isn’t separate from the rest of the job.
sentences.zh: 这就是我希望我的受训者明白的：发现值得解决的问题与工作的其余部分是不可分割的。

sentences.en: It comes from staying engaged with people’s work long enough to see what no single request can show you.
sentences.zh: 它来自于与人们的工作保持足够长的时间，以了解任何单一请求都无法向您展示什么。

content_html_zh:
注意：根据读者的反馈，本文在发布后进行了修改，以提高清晰度。

“你如何发现值得解决的问题？” 我导师的一位高级工程师最近问我。 他试图晋升为高级工程师，并意识到这个角色不仅仅是完成分配给他的工作。 他还需要参与弄清楚他的团队和组织应该构建什么。

其他人建议他在日历上留出时间来思考更大的前景。 他尝试过，但没有发现有效，所以他问我是否有其他选择。

我告诉他，我很少通过盯着空白页并试图“战略性思考”来找到好的问题。 相反，我表现得像一块海绵。 我倾听日常的噪音，吸收人们遇到的问题，并让它们留在我的脑海中。 随着时间的推移，一些人逐渐消失，而另一些人之间开始出现最初看似无关的联系。 最终，我开始明白是什么真正让人们放慢了脚步，以及我或我的团队可以做些什么。

我曾与许多从未真正尝试过这一点的工程师一起工作过。 他们等待经理或领导发现机会，然后通过解决最困难的问题来展示他们的价值。 这绝对可以带来晋升。 但在我的职业生涯中给我留下最深刻印象的项目是那些我发现并解决了我的领导尚未意识到的重要问题的项目。

需要注意的是：我的经验主要来自在大公司的基础设施和开发人员工具方面的工作，以及在工程师拥有大量自下而上的自主权来影响他们的路线图的团队中的工作。 在更加自上而下的环境中，这种方式的工作空间可能会更小。

吸收问题，而不是请求

人们喜欢谈论他们面临的问题：在会议、聊天、演示和电子邮件中。 他们解释为什么他们的工作很辛苦，抱怨是什么让他们放慢了脚步，并描述了他们希望自己能做什么。

当有东西与我的区域重叠时，我开始拉线。 我可能会问，“如果 X 存在，它能解决你的问题吗？” 或者向他们指出我拥有的产品中的现有功能，并询问该功能涵盖了他们的多少用例。

用户经常要求特定的解决方案，而不是解释其根本问题。 我不会只看表面上的要求，而是不断挖掘，直到了解他们想要实现的目标以及为什么现有产品不适合他们。

作为一个天生内向的人，这种环境聆听对我来说特别有效。 我不需要为了寻找想法而在日程表上塞满推测性的会议；在正常的一周里，我周围已经有大量有用的信息在流动。

然而，当一个问题似乎值得探索时，我会变得更加积极；我需要看看它如何影响团队的日常工作。 当他们向我介绍他们的工作流程以及他们正在调查的错误时，我会和他们坐在一起。 如果可以的话，我会尝试自己解决其中一些错误。 直接看到问题可以更轻松地将团队实际需要的内容与他们要求的解决方案分开。

我还寻找比我更了解组织的人：那些拥有关键系统、跨多个团队工作或对我团队下游工作有特别深入了解的人。 我会安排一对一或咖啡聊天，询问他们遇到的有趣问题。 他们可能已经在多个地方看到了同样的问题，并开始将这些点联系起来，让我在模式上领先一步，否则我可能需要更长时间才能注意到。

让问题不断积累

有好几次，我因动作太快而被烫伤。 我对一个声音团队的请求感到兴奋，构建了这个功能，然后看着他们几乎不使用它。 他们的优先事项发生了变化，或者请求来自不再重要的一次性调查。 团队在那一刻的渴望程度并不等同于该功能相对于我的产品需要支持的其他所有内容的重要性。 由于过度关注他们的要求，我忽视了更大的前景。

这教会了我要让潜在的问题堆积起来。 按照我的方式倾听，我遇到的问题远远超出了我所能解决的范围，而且并非所有问题都值得采取行动。 大多数人不需要在我第一次听说它们时就将其转变为项目；等待可以是一种超能力。

等待意味着相同的问题可能会在不同的团队中独立出现，从而使其成为更优先解决的问题。 或者表面上看起来不同的问题可能最终具有相同的形状，因此我可以一次性解决多个用例。 或者，正如我痛苦地了解到的那样，提出请求的团队一开始根本就没有那么在意。

相反，我会在心里记下并在问题再次出现时重新审视该问题。 我认识的其他工程师更系统地记录了这类事情。 该机制是个人选择：每个人都必须找出适合自己的机制。 重要的是让未解决的问题保持足够长的时间，以便积累更多证据。

找出共同的形状

等待可以帮助我收集证据，但仅凭这一点并不能告诉我要构建什么。 我仍然需要弄清楚我保留的问题是否真正相关，如果有的话，可以一起解决它们。

我使用的性能调试工具 Perfetto 就是一个很好的例子。 它在由称为“轨道”的行组成的时间线上显示系统活动的记录。 几年来，团队不断要求对 UI 进行小的、具体的添加。 人们想要一个命令来将他们喜欢的曲目固定在屏幕顶部；下一个团队想要同样的东西，但要制作一组完全不同的曲目。 其他人希望 Perfetto 打开已经放大的录音的特定部分，或者显示根据他们关心的内容调整的自定义聚合。 一些人已经停止等待我们，并使用书签构建了精心设计的解决方法。1

当这些都堆积起来时，我的头脑又像往常一样混乱：请求本身、每个请求的限制以及一些半成形的解决方案。 我学会了不要仅仅坐在办公桌前思考来强迫解决方案。 相反，我最好的解开纠结的方式是在伦敦漫无目的地散步，当我不试图强迫他们时，联系会更容易。

我最终意识到，这些团队中没有一个真正想要他们所要求的特定功能。 每个人都希望针对自己的工作流程个性化 Perfetto，而不是将自己的选择强加给其他人。 根本需求不是任何一项功能，而是扩展 UI 的能力。 当这样的联系最终产生时，这是工作中最好的感觉之一：几个尴尬的请求崩溃成一个想法，并且出现了他们自己都没有暗示过的可能性。

然而，这种感觉正是我必须小心的时候，因为常见的形状只是一个假设，优雅并不是证据。 当扩展 UI 时，它被证明是真实的，但我以前被愚弄过。

在最近的另一个案例中，我确信构建一个用于查询 Perfetto 跟踪的透明缓存系统将解决共享大型跟踪和重复查询的问题。 直到我编写 RFC 并构建原型时，我才意识到这种优雅是一个谎言：这两个问题需要真正不同的解决方案。 我不情愿地将设计分成两部分，两半都已发货。2

施工前进行压力测试

你可能认为这就是我开始构建的时刻，但通常不是。 我能走多远取决于我对这个想法是否有效以及人们是否真正想要它的确信程度。

如果某件事有用且风险足够低，我会立即采取行动：发送更改并让我的经理知道。 当我不确定一个想法是否可行或需要付出多少努力时，我会构建一个一次性原型；它暴露了失败点，并为我提供了一些具体的内容供其他人做出反应。 当一个想法很大但我被它说服时，我会全力以赴：数周或数月的工作以及在其他工程师和团队之间建立支持的艰苦努力。

通过这一切，我不仅试图说服其他人，而且还试图说服其他人。我也在努力说服自己。 有时，诚实的答案是停止：如果人们看不到我所做的价值，或者我们遇到了主要的技术障碍，我宁愿现在放弃这个想法，也不愿构建一些没有人使用或成为维护噩梦的东西。 有时它会持续下去，但时机不对，所以我把它搁置起来，准备在它成为组织优先事项的那一天立即采取行动。

当一个想法确实成立时，我不一定是构建它的人。 我可能会实施它，我团队中的其他人可能会实施它，或者它可能会改变组织的重点。 即使我不负责实施，找到并塑造正确的问题也会产生影响。

Perfetto 扩展的想法值得全力以赴。 我们已经在构建插件来模块化 UI，但它们还不够：团队必须开源所有插件代码，这对于许多内部用例来说不是一个选择。 因此，在构建任何新产品之前，我将问题和建议提交给我的经理、队友和客户团队。 我最终写了两份 RFC，进行了几次一对一讨论并进行了几次演讲，并根据反馈进行了改进。

最后，我将宏设计并实现为“轻量级扩展”：一种无需编写插件即可在 UI 中自动执行操作的方法。 扩展服务器通过让团队共享他们的宏来进一步发展这个想法。

我们没有自己实现每个要求的功能，而是为团队提供了根据自己的需求调整 Perfetto 的方法。 Google 内部的数十个团队现在使用宏和扩展服务器，其他几家公司也在内部使用扩展服务器。

解决有用的问题可以帮助我找到下一个问题

我越经常经历这个过程，它就会变得越容易。 当我对某人的问题表现出真正的兴趣、提出有用的问题或帮助解决问题时，他们会记住。 他们开始更早地来找我，让我与面临相关问题的其他人进行对话。

这让我能够更广泛地了解整个组织正在发生的事情，从而更容易发现模式并构建人们真正需要的东西。 解决其中一个问题会让我进行更多对话，并且循环继续。

这些成功建立了来自长期管理的信任。 早期，我必须亲自将其中许多想法变成现实，以证明我的判断是正确的。 随着时间的推移，我的经理和组织更加重视我对重要事项的评估。 这使我能够影响路线图，而无需拥有每个项目。

这与成为一名高级工程师意味着用会议和协调取代技术工作的想法不同。 对我来说，对话是对我构建的内容的输入，而不是最终结果。

结论

这就是我希望我的受训者明白的：发现值得解决的问题与工作的其余部分是不可分割的。 它来自于与人们的工作保持足够长的时间，以了解任何单一请求都无法向您展示什么。
